chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Chamber Under the Lawn
Chapter 9: The Music of the Spheres
Back Matter: Papers from the Winter

spans.text: The fourteenth of March, eighteen eighty-one, and the morning was better than the four before it, which was the only reason any of the rest of it happened.

Eleanor Atherton knew about mornings like that by then. They were not recoveries. They were loans, and she had stopped being grateful for them in about November and had started, instead, to spend them, which she considered a considerable improvement in her character and did not mention to anybody.

She was awake at six. By half past she had established that she could stand. Then that she could dress. Then that she could get down the west stair on one hand and not two. Each was a separate question. She asked all three and did not hurry any of them.

Then she went out through the garden door, because the garden door was on the west side and nobody in that house used the west side any more, and she walked half a mile across the south park to the aviary.

It took her one hour and forty minutes. It was, on any reasonable measure, the most foolish thing she did in the last year of her life. She stopped eleven times. She sat down twice, once on the stile and once on the grass, which she had not intended and did not enjoy. A man cutting the hedge on the far side of the ha-ha saw her go and did not call out. She had been walking that park at odd hours for twelve years. The men had decided among themselves a long time ago that it was not their business.
She got there at twenty past eight and let herself in with her own key.

Her mother had built the aviary in the year Eleanor turned twelve. She had died in the year Eleanor turned nineteen. In between she had spent a great deal of money on a glass dome in a park, and had been laughed at for it at dinner tables in three counties.
The glass was cold. The chorus was silent, because the chorus was always silent unless somebody wound it, and Eleanor did not wind it, because she wanted the quiet.
She sat down on the iron bench for eleven minutes and got her breath back.
Then she took the feather out of her pocket.
It was a primary, cream and rose. It had been on the floor of the aviary in the autumn. She had picked it up and kept it five months without deciding what it was for.
She had known perfectly well what it was for.
She had not been prepared to say so. Saying so meant admitting the whole arrangement to herself in one piece, and she had been letting herself have it in parts.

The note was already written. It was a strip of paper the width of two fingers and it had cost her four attempts and the best part of an evening, and what it said in the end was fourteen words that a child could read.
She wired it to the spine of the feather with brass wire, sitting on the bench with the light coming down grey through the dome. She made a bad job of it twice. The third time it held.
Her hands were not what they had been. That was the thing she minded most and she had told nobody, and there was nobody to tell.

The panel was under the middle of the disc, cut into the stone and fitted flush, and it came up on its own when the chorus ran down and at no other time. She had found that out when she was fourteen, by being in the building alone and winding the thing to see what it did. A child left alone in a building learns every moving part of it. It had never once occurred to her, in seventeen years, that the knowledge was worth anything.

She wound the chorus and sat through the whole of it and let the panel come up on its own. Then she put the feather in with the note wired to it, and she did not lay it flat. She set it with the vane standing proud of the lip, because the whole of the idea was that it should not stay there. When the chorus ran, the air over the disc moved. She had sat under it as a girl and watched the dust turn in it. A feather set that way would lift, and it would go up in front of whoever happened to be standing in the room, and they would not have had to be looking for it. That was the entire point and it was the part she was least willing to say out loud. The panel went back down as the spring came off it, and she pressed it with the flat of her hand until it sat true.
Then she stood in the middle of the floor and looked up.

Nine small dark squares on the north half of the dome. Nine on the south. She looked at them for a while and did not say anything, because there was nobody there and she was not in the habit of talking to herself.
She had one clear thought while she was standing there and she wrote it down that night, and it was not about the feather.
If it is found by somebody who is looking for it, I have wasted a morning. If it is found by somebody who is simply paying attention, then I have done the thing properly.
She was carried back.
She had not planned that and she resented it for about a day and a half. The hedge man came across the park at ten and found her on the grass again, three hundred yards short of the terrace.

He did not ask her whether she wanted assistance. She thought afterward that it was the most tactful act of her adult life. He came and stood there and said he was going up to the house in any case, and would she care to come along, and gave her his arm.

His name was Bright. She had known him since she was nine. He had taught her the names of four trees and she had taught him to read the numbers on a seed packet, when they were both children and it had not yet been explained to either of them why they should not.
He did not ask her where she had been. He talked instead, the whole way, about a wall.
It is going,
spans.speaker: Bright

spans.text: said Bright.
Which.
The one along the top of the hanger. Forty rod of it.
He set a slow pace and did not appear to be setting one.
It has been going since your father’s time. I have had it up twice and it has come down twice and I have stopped telling anybody.
Why has it come down.
Because it is built on nothing.
spans.speaker: Bright

spans.text: Bright said it with some satisfaction.

There is no foot to it. Somebody run it up in a hurry a long while back and put the stone straight on the ground, and you may build as good a wall as you like on top of nothing and it will still be a wall on top of nothing.
spans.speaker: Bright

spans.text: Can it be mended.
It can be took down and done proper.
Then why has nobody.
Because it is forty rod and it is out of sight of the house,
spans.speaker: Bright

spans.text: said Bright,
and a thing out of sight of the house does not get done.
spans.speaker: Bright

spans.text: Eleanor walked another thirty yards.
That is the truest sentence anybody has said to me this year,
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: she said.
It is about a wall, miss.
I am aware of what it is about.

Bright thought about that for a while, and then said that she had always been a peculiar child, and that he had said so at the time and been told off for it. Eleanor said that he had been quite right. They got to the terrace at about a quarter to eleven and he took his arm back and went off round the end of the house without saying goodbye, which she was grateful for.
She slept from twelve until four.
The room they had put her in that winter was on the second floor of the west wing, and it was small, and it was painted green.

It faced the rose garden, which was the reason it had been chosen, and it had been chosen by her brother, and he had told her so himself, standing in the doorway with his hat in his hand, in December. He had said it would be better for her to be in the house. He had said the cottage was damp. Both were true. He had meant them. She had thanked him.
Neither of them said one word about the twelve years, and neither of them was ever going to.
There was a bell.

It was on the wall beside the fireplace. It went through to the board in the passage behind the kitchen. It was labelled, because every bell in that house was labelled, in a small upright hand that some clerk had put there before any of them were born.

She had rung it four times since December. Twice for the fire and twice because she had needed help and had run out of ways of not needing it. On the fourteenth of March she wanted the candle moved and did not ring, and got up and moved it herself, and sat down again feeling rather pleased and rather ridiculous.
Agnes came at six.

Agnes was eleven and was her brother’s elder girl, and she came most days, and it had never once been arranged. Nobody had told her to. Nobody, as far as Eleanor could establish, had told her not to either, which was the family all over.
That evening she brought a wren’s egg in a twist of cotton wool and put it on the table and did not say anything about it, and waited to be asked.
Where,
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: said Eleanor.
Under the wall by the pump. It was broken already. I did not take it off anything.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: How many were there.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: Six. Five went.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: Agnes sat down on the fender.
I counted them out over four days. The fifth one went on Thursday and I waited two more days before I came, in case the sixth one was late, and it was not late, it was dead.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: Eleanor looked at her for a moment.

There were, she thought, a great many children in the world who would have brought her the egg. There were considerably fewer who would have waited two days before deciding what it meant, and fewer still who would have said five went rather than five hatched, having not seen them hatch.
That is the right way to do it,
she said.
Do what.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: Count a thing you cannot see the end of.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: Eleanor turned the twist of cotton wool over with one finger and did not pick it up.
You said five went. You did not say five hatched.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: I did not see them hatch.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: No. And most grown people would have written down that five hatched, because it is what happened, and because it is a nicer sentence.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: Eleanor looked at her.
You put in what you watched and you left out the rest. Who taught you that.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: Agnes considered the question seriously, which was her way, and took some time over it.
Nobody,
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: she said.
It is only that if you put in the part you did not see, then afterwards you cannot tell which part was which.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: No.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: And then the whole of it is no use.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: Agnes pulled her feet up onto the fender.

I did that with the swallows. I wrote down when they came and I had not been there for two days at the start and I put a day in that I had guessed at, and the next year I could not tell which day was the guessed one, and I had to throw the whole page away.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: How old were you.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: Nine.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: And you have not done it since.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: I have not done it since,
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: said Agnes.
Eleanor sat back.
There was a thing she wanted very much to say and she did not say it. The not saying it cost her more than the walk had.

She had been given, at the very end, a child in this house who counted properly. She had rather less than a year. And there was no version of the arrangement in which telling her anything was a kindness.
Will you do something for me,
she said instead.
Yes.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: You have not asked what it is.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: You will tell me,
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: said Agnes.
I am going to give you a book. Not tonight. Before the summer.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: Eleanor kept her voice entirely level.
It is a bird book and it was my mother’s and there is a good deal written in the margins, some of it by me when I was smaller than you, and most of it is not worth reading.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: May I read it anyway.
spans.speaker: Agnes

spans.text: You may do anything you like with it. That is what giving means.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: Eleanor picked up the wren’s egg at last and set it carefully back in its cotton wool.
I would only ask that you keep it. Not look after it. Keep it. There is a difference and you will find it out.
spans.speaker: Eleanor

spans.text: Agnes nodded, in the manner of somebody accepting a straightforward commission, and then asked whether Eleanor wanted the fire made up, and made it up, and went at seven because she was made to go at seven.
The letter took her until nearly eleven.

She had drafted it three times in February and burned two of the drafts, and what she wrote that night was mostly the third one with the self-pity taken out, which had been the whole of the work. It ran to four sides. She wrote it at the small table with one candle, because two made her eyes ache by then. She wrote it in one sitting. She had learned in January that she could no longer rely on being the same person two days running.
She did not read it back. She had decided that in advance and she held to it.
At about a quarter past eleven she put the pen down and opened the window.

It was cold and the rose garden was black and she could not see anything at all, and she stood there with her hand on the frame, and after perhaps two minutes, from somewhere down towards the yew hedge, a thrush began.
It was the first of that spring.
She had heard the first thrush of the spring in that park every year since she was seven. Every year but one. The one was eighteen sixty-nine.
And she had written the date down every time, in the margin of a book, in the same book. When she was small she had written the date and the weather. Once, memorably, a complaint about her brother.
She listened to the whole of it. It went on for a good while and then stopped, in the way they do, in the middle of the phrase rather than at the end of it.
Then she shut the window and got the bird book out of the drawer.

It was the one her mother had given her and it had her mother’s name in the front and Eleanor had never written her own underneath it, which she had meant to do for twenty years. The song thrush plate was near the front. The four April lines she had put in the margin as a child were still there. The hand was round and slow and pressed far too hard, and she could hardly believe it had ever been hers.
She did not write on that page. She had not written on that page since she was a girl.
She turned instead to the plate she had been using since, further back, and found the last thing she had put there, which had been in the autumn, and looked at the gap under it for a while.
Then she wrote the date, and two words, and her initials.
One more.
She looked at it. It was not what she had thought she was going to write and she did not cross it out.
She put the pen down.
The book stayed open on her knees. The letter lay on the table beside her, four sides of it, folded once. The candle was going. Outside the window the rose garden was black.
It was a small green room, in a wing of a house that nobody used.
